paras: The lynching of John Stroman was the killing of a Black man by a citizen posse near Wharton, Texas, in August 1895, after he was accused of shooting Deputy Sheriff Frank Brown. The posse that held him reported that he had "escaped," but a later Wharton dispatch said he had been lynched below town and buried. The same dispatch said the "unwritten law" had been invoked and that there was very little comment.

According to Sheriff R. A. Rich, six convicts had escaped from the Caney State farm in Matagorda county, and his deputies were told to keep watch. Deputy Frank Brown, at the home of his father-in-law Andrew Kemp, questioned a Black man who came to the well for water and, suspicious, set out to take him to town handcuffed by one wrist to his saddle rope. The mail hack driver later found Brown dead on the road about five miles below Wharton.

Drawing on the inquest held by Justice Whitten, the sheriff said the man shot Brown in the back with a concealed pistol, fired the deputy's shotgun, and left with his spurs, gun and mare. A wire report described the wanted man as a "mulatto" convict sent from Lamar county for grand larceny and said Rich offered $100 for his capture.

While large posses searched the county, Bob Golbraith, Banks Barbee and Albert Paul found the man gambling with other Black men on the lower Brooks place, arrested him, and guarded him overnight. Early the next morning they turned him over to another posse, which started for town but reported on arrival that the prisoner had escaped. Constable Hearit, who rode to catch up with the posse, was told the same, and the search was called off. A Post reporter heard that the prisoner had confessed to the killing and told where he had hidden the deputy's gun.
A dispatch dated August 22 stated that the man "was lynched Tuesday night below town" for Brown's murder.

Sergeant C. F. Patton of the State farm and Sheriff Rich had the body exhumed, and Patton concluded that the man was not an escaped convict. The man had given his name as John Stroman and was said to be wanted in Brazoria county for stealing the race mare Crazy Jane. Citizens "unanimously" cleared the sheriff of failing to secure the prisoner, and no inquest, arrest or prosecution for the lynching appears in the coverage.

Coverage came from Texas white papers, chiefly the Fort Worth Gazette, which printed Wharton correspondence to the Post. Its first item, headed "Said He Escaped," put the posse's word "escaped" in quotation marks under the subhead "Negro Murderer Is Probably Lynched by His Captors." The Austin Weekly Statesman reprinted that item as "Captured and Escaped," while the Shiner Gazette carried only the first wire on Brown's death under "Killed His Captor."

The Wharton correspondent called Brown's death a "brutal murder," mourned him as "beloved and respected," and referred to the accused as "the murderer" throughout. Reporting the lynching, the same correspondent wrote that the crime was so brutal that the "unwritten law" was invoked "and that ended it." No Black-press report of the episode was found.

The posse's claim of an escape was contradicted by the later local report of a lynching, which was written after the body had been exhumed. The man's identity also shifted, from an escaped Caney farm convict, or a Lamar county "mulatto" in the wire version, to a horse-theft suspect named John Stroman. The dates differ as well: the first dispatch, dated August 19, placed the capture the night before, while the August 22 dispatch put the lynching on Tuesday night, August 20.

reader.title: Lynching of John Stroman
bases: A Black man held by a citizen posse after the killing of a deputy sheriff was reported 'escaped' and was later described as 'lynched' and buried below Wharton (A1, A2, A5).

A later Wharton dispatch states the prisoner 'was lynched' and his body buried, after posses of citizens (the capturing party alone numbered three named men) failed to deliver him to town (A2, A5). The killing was presented as punishment for the deputy's murder under the 'unwritten law' (A5).

Only the Aug. 22 Wharton correspondence states that the man was lynched (A5); the earlier wire carried the posse's 'escaped' claim with only a headline surmise of lynching (A1), and the other reports concern the deputy's killing and the capture (A2, A4).

framing.detail: The Fort Worth Gazette reported the posse's 'escaped' claim in quotation marks under the headline 'Probably Lynched by His Captors' while calling the accused the 'Negro Murderer'.
The Post correspondence printed in the Gazette called the deputy's death a 'brutal murder' and said 'the crime was of such a brutal nature that the "unwritten law" was invoked and that ended it'.
The Austin Weekly Statesman reprinted the Aug. 19 special under 'Captured and Escaped.'
The Shiner Gazette ran only the first wire on the killing of Brown and the pursuit, headed 'Killed His Captor.'
